items.title: Garbage collection and ownership both manage memory
items.claim: Java and Python use garbage collection; C requires manual memory management. Rust takes a third approach. Which is it?

options.text: Rust uses garbage collection like Java
Rust uses an ownership and borrow-checking system enforced at compile time; memory is freed deterministically when the owning variable goes out of scope, with no runtime GC

items.reveal:
Rust's ownership model (one owner, borrowing rules) prevents use-after-free, double-free and data races at compile time. Graydon Hoare started Rust at Mozilla in 2006; it reached 1.0 in 2015.

Microsoft's 2019 analysis of its CVEs found ~70% were memory safety bugs in C/C++. The Linux kernel began accepting Rust modules in 2022. Android's 2023 report noted memory-safety vulnerabilities dropped from 76% (2019) to 24% (2023) as code moved to memory-safe languages.
items.why: Memory safety can be enforced at compile time, runtime (GC) or by programmer discipline. The choice trades performance, predictability and ergonomics.

items.title: 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
items.claim: In most programming languages using IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic, what does 0.1 + 0.2 evaluate to?
items.reveal:
Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation. The standard IEEE 754 double evaluates the sum to 0.30000000000000004.

Decimal or arbitrary-precision libraries are used where this matters (finance, audit).
items.why: Numerical errors emerge from representation, not arithmetic mistakes.
